messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rahul, a 61-year-old paramedic of South Asian descent, had spent decades serving his community with dedication and precision. However, it was during one fateful emergency response that his life took a drastic turn. While treating a patient who had been exposed to toxic chemicals, Rahul himself inhaled the noxious fumes, leaving him shaken and forever changed. In the weeks that followed, Rahul found himself increasingly uneasy whenever he entered dark spaces or caught a whiff of alcohol – smells eerily reminiscent of the chemicals he had encountered that day. These triggers would send his mind reeling back to the traumatic event, and he'd feel the same terror wash over him as if it were happening all over again. To cope with these overwhelming memories, Rahul began to ruminate on how the event could have been prevented, replaying every detail in his head like a mantra. These ruminations led Rahul to become withdrawn from his work and social life, afraid of being alone with his thoughts or confronting medical cues that might transport him back to that fateful day. He started surrounding himself with people constantly, whether it was at the hospital or in social gatherings, just so he wouldn't be left to face his memories head-on. His wife noticed a change in him and tried to reassure Rahul that everything would be okay, but he couldn't shake off the feeling of dread that clung to him like a shroud. As time passed, the smallest reminders – the smell of disinfectant at the hospital or the sound of sirens in the distance – could instantly bring back the full memory of that terrible day without warning. When this happened, Rahul felt the same suffocating overwhelm he'd experienced during the event itself. His colleagues started to notice his erratic behavior and avoidance tactics, but Rahul couldn't help it; every time he recalled the trauma, the emotions came flooding back like a tidal wave. Rahul's avoidance of medical cues had another unintended consequence: his performance at work began to suffer. He'd hesitate during critical situations or freeze up when faced with patients who required urgent care – all because the memories of that traumatic event lingered, threatening to consume him whole. His self-doubt grew, and so did his reliance on rumination as a coping mechanism. One day, Rahul's wife sat him down for a heart-to-heart conversation, expressing her concerns about his deteriorating mental health. She gently pointed out how his avoidance behaviors were affecting not only his work but also their relationship and daily life together. For the first time in months, Rahul let his guard down, allowing himself to confront the memories he'd been desperately trying to suppress. As he opened up to his wife, Rahul realized that his efforts to avoid the past had ultimately led him further into its clutches. He knew then that it was time to seek professional help – not just for himself but also for those who loved and cared about him. With a mix of trepidation and determination, Rahul decided to take the first step towards healing, hoping to break free from the suffocating grip of his memories and learn to confront the trauma head-on.
